question: Who was the founder of the Sunga dynasty, which succeeded the Mauryas in Magadha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pushyamitra Sunga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pushyamitra Sunga, the commander-in-chief of the last Mauryan king Brihadratha, seized the throne around 185 BC and founded the Sunga dynasty (पुष्यमित्र शुंग — शुंग वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• The Sunga capital was Pataliputra, with Vidisha (Vidhisha) also serving as an important seat of the dynasty.

 

• Pushyamitra is said to have performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices, with the learned grammarian Patanjali as priest.

 

• The dynasty was the first major power to rule the Gangetic plain after the fall of the Mauryas.

 

• It was ended when the last ruler Devabhuti was murdered by his minister Vasudeva Kanva.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sunga period is also remembered for the expansion and enrichment of the Buddhist stupas at Bharhut and Sanchi.

 

• The Besnagar Garuda pillar was erected by the Greek envoy Heliodorus in Sunga territory around Vidisha.

 

• Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitra has the Sunga prince Agnimitra as its hero.

 

• The Sunga rulers governed a territory smaller than the Mauryan empire, centred on the middle Ganga valley and parts of central India.

 

NOTE

 

• Agnimitra (Option 1): Agnimitra was the son of Pushyamitra and became the second Sunga ruler after his father's death. He was a successor, not the founder, of the dynasty, and is the hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitra.

 

• Vasudeva Kanva (Option 2): Vasudeva Kanva was the minister of the last Sunga king who murdered him and founded the later Kanva dynasty. He therefore ended the Sunga line rather than starting it.

 

• Devabhuti (Option 3): Devabhuti was the tenth and last Sunga ruler, who was killed by his own minister. He marks the end of the dynasty, so he cannot be its founder.

question: The Mahabhasya, a famous commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi, was written by the priest of Pushyamitra Sunga. Who was he?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Patanjali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Patanjali was the royal priest (Purohit) of Pushyamitra Sunga and wrote the Mahabhasya, the great commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi; he conducted Pushyamitra's Ashvamedha sacrifices (पतंजलि — महाभाष्य, पुष्यमित्र शुंग के पुरोहित)

 

• Panini composed the Ashtadhyayi, the foundational Sanskrit grammar of about 4000 sutras.

 

• Patanjali is also traditionally credited with the Yoga Sutras, the basic text of the Yoga school.

 

• The Mahabhasya is valuable as a source for the society and language of the Sunga age.

 

• Pushyamitra is said to have performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices, a revival of Vedic ritual.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Panini's grammar -> Katyayana's Vartika -> Patanjali's Mahabhasya form the three stages of Sanskrit grammar (the 'Munitraya').

 

• Patanjali's Yoga Sutras systematise the eight-fold path (Ashtanga Yoga).

 

• Patanjali's references to the Yavana attack on Saketa and Madhyamika are used by historians to date events of his age.

 

• Patanjali also mentions contemporary events such as a Yavana attack, which historians use to date Sunga events.

 

NOTE

 

• Kautilya (Option 1): Kautilya (Chanakya) was the minister of Chandragupta Maurya and the author of the Arthashastra on statecraft. He belongs to the Mauryan age, centuries before the Sunga priest who wrote the Mahabhasya.

 

• Katyayana (Option 3): Katyayana wrote Vartikas, short explanatory notes on Panini's rules, and thus came between Panini and Patanjali. He was not the priest of Pushyamitra and did not write the Mahabhasya.

 

• Charaka (Option 4): Charaka was the court physician of Kanishka and the author of the Charaka Samhita on medicine. He has no connection with Sanskrit grammar or the Sunga court.

question: Who was the last ruler of the Sunga dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Devabhuti.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Devabhuti was the last ruler of the Sunga dynasty; he was murdered by his own minister, who then seized the throne and started a new dynasty (देवभूति — अंतिम शुंग शासक)

 

• His killer, Vasudeva Kanva, founded the Kanva dynasty around 73 BC with Pataliputra as capital.

 

• Devabhuti is described by tradition as a weak and pleasure-loving king, which helped the minister's coup.

 

• The Sungas ruled for roughly a century (about 185 BC to 73 BC).

 

• The Kanva dynasty that followed lasted only about 45 years.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sunga line began with Pushyamitra and included Agnimitra, Vasumitra, Bhagabhadra (in whose reign Heliodorus came to Vidisha) and others.

 

• The Sunga period saw the rise of Brahmanical ritual along with continued Buddhist art at Bharhut and Sanchi.

 

• After the Kanvas, the Satavahanas became the leading power in the Deccan.

 

NOTE

 

• Vasudeva (Option 2): Vasudeva was the founder of the Kanva dynasty and the minister who killed the last Sunga king. He was a Kanva, not a Sunga, so he cannot be the last Sunga ruler.

 

• Pushyamitra Sunga (Option 3): Pushyamitra Sunga was the founder and first ruler of the dynasty, who took the throne from the last Maurya. The question asks for the final ruler, who came about a century later.

 

• Agnimitra (Option 4): Agnimitra was the son and immediate successor of Pushyamitra, so he was the second Sunga ruler. He appears at the beginning, not the end, of the dynasty.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Sunga dynasty:

1. Pushyamitra Sunga performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices.

2. Pataliputra and Vidisha were important centres of the dynasty.

3. The dynasty was founded by Vasudeva.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Correct statements are 1 and 2: Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices and the Sungas ruled from Pataliputra / Vidisha; statement 3 is false because the founder was Pushyamitra (शुंग वंश — दो अश्वमेध यज्ञ, पाटलिपुत्र/विदिशा)

 

• Vasudeva was the founder of the Kanva dynasty, which replaced the Sungas.

 

• The priest at Pushyamitra's sacrifices was Patanjali, author of the Mahabhasya.

 

• Ashvamedha sacrifices were Vedic rituals meant to proclaim the king's paramount power.

 

• Pushyamitra took power from the last Mauryan king Brihadratha.

 

• Pushyamitra's Ashvamedha sacrifices reflected a revival of Vedic ritual after the Mauryan patronage of Buddhism.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pushyamitra's son Agnimitra was the hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitra.

 

• Vasumitra, grandson of Pushyamitra, is described in tradition as defeating the Yavanas on the Indus.

 

• The Sunga rulers are credited with additions to the stupa railings at Bharhut.

 

• Sunga rule lasted about 112 years in the traditional Puranic reckoning, from about 185 BC to 73 BC, with ten kings listed.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This choice includes statement 3 along with statement 2 as correct. Statement 3 is wrong, since Vasudeva founded the Kanva dynasty and not the Sungas, so this combination cannot be right.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This option leaves out statement 1 and wrongly keeps statement 3. Pushyamitra did perform two Ashvamedha sacrifices, and statement 3 about Vasudeva as Sunga founder is false.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): This answer marks all three statements as correct, but statement 3 is false because Vasudeva was the founder of the Kanvas, so the full set cannot be correct.

question: Who succeeded Pushyamitra Sunga on the throne after his death?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Agnimitra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Agnimitra, the son of Pushyamitra Sunga, became king after his father's death; he is the hero of Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitra (अग्निमित्र — पुष्यमित्र का पुत्र)

 

• Before becoming king he served as the viceroy at Vidisha under his father.

 

• The play Malavikagnimitra describes his love for the exiled princess Malavika and also refers to the wars of the Sunga period.

 

• Pushyamitra's grandson Vasumitra is said in the same tradition to have defeated the Yavanas on the banks of the Sindhu.

 

• The line ended with Devabhuti, the last Sunga ruler.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalidasa's other works include Abhijnanashakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam, Raghuvamsha, Meghaduta and Kumarasambhava.

 

• Malavikagnimitra is a Sanskrit drama of five acts and is an important literary source for Sunga history.

 

• Vidisha (near Besnagar and Sanchi) was an important city in the Sunga domain.

 

• Malavikagnimitra is a five-act Sanskrit play by Kalidasa and is among the literary sources for Sunga history and court life.

 

NOTE

 

• Devabhuti (Option 2): Devabhuti was the last Sunga king, ruling about a century later. He was killed by his minister, so he cannot be the immediate successor of the founder.

 

• Vasumitra (Option 3): Vasumitra was Pushyamitra's grandson and a prince famed for fighting the Yavanas, but the throne passed first to Agnimitra, Pushyamitra's son, and not to him.

 

• Susharman (Option 4): Susharman was the last Kanva ruler, who came after the Sungas had been overthrown. He belongs to a different dynasty and a later age.

question: The founder of the Kanva dynasty, who overthrew the last Sunga ruler, was:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vasudeva Kanva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vasudeva Kanva, minister of the last Sunga king Devabhuti, killed him and founded the Kanva dynasty with its capital at Pataliputra (वासुदेव कण्व — कण्व वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• The Kanvas were Brahmins by origin, and the dynasty lasted only about 45 years.

 

• The Puranas list four Kanva kings: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana and Susharman.

 

• The last Kanva king, Susharman, was overthrown by the Satavahana founder Simuka according to tradition.

 

• Kanva rule covered only a shrunken Magadha as the Satavahanas rose in the Deccan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kanvas ruled from roughly 73 BC to 28 BC.

 

• Their fall opened the way for Satavahana expansion into central India.

 

• After the Kanvas, no powerful ruler arose in Magadha until the rise of the Guptas.

 

• Because the Kanvas came to power by a ministerial coup, they are often treated as a short, weak interlude between the Sungas and the Satavahanas.

 

NOTE

 

• Simuka (Option 1): Simuka was the founder of the Satavahana dynasty in the Deccan and is said to have destroyed the last Kanva king. He was a rival power, not the founder of the Kanvas.

 

• Susharman (Option 3): Susharman was the last Kanva king, ruling at the very end of the dynasty. He was not the founder, since the dynasty began with Vasudeva decades earlier.

 

• Bhumimitra (Option 4): Bhumimitra was the son and successor of Vasudeva, so he was the second Kanva ruler. He inherited a dynasty already founded by his father.

question: Who was the last ruler of the Kanva dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Susharman.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Susharman was the last ruler of the Kanva dynasty; tradition says he was killed by Simuka, founder of the Satavahana line (सुशर्मन — अंतिम कण्व शासक)

 

• With his fall the Kanva rule in Magadha ended after only about 45 years.

 

• The Kanvas had followed the Sungas, whose last ruler was Devabhuti.

 

• The Satavahanas then grew into the main power of the Deccan.

 

• The Kanvas were Brahmin rulers who controlled only a small part of the former Mauryan heartland.

 

• After Susharman the Kanva rule ended and the Satavahanas rose as the leading power in the Deccan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanva rulers: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana and Susharman.

 

• The Satavahana rule is placed roughly from the 1st century BC to the 3rd century AD.

 

• The Satavahanas are also called the Andhras in the Puranas.

 

• The Puranas record that the Kanvas were Brahmins by caste, and that their kings held only a small territory around Magadha and eastern central India.

 

NOTE

 

• Devabhuti (Option 1): Devabhuti was the last Sunga king, not a Kanva. He was killed by Vasudeva Kanva, who started the Kanva line that later ended with Susharman.

 

• Vasudeva (Option 2): Vasudeva was the first Kanva king and the founder of the dynasty. The question asks about the last ruler, who came decades after him.

 

• Yajna Sri Satakarni (Option 3): Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great Satavahana ruler, a much later figure of the Deccan. He did not rule Magadha and was not a Kanva.

question: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Kanva dynasty?
option_1: It was founded by Vasudeva Kanva
option_3: It was founded by Pushyamitra Sunga
solution_text:
The correct answer is It was founded by Pushyamitra Sunga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The statement that the Kanva dynasty was founded by Pushyamitra Sunga is incorrect, because Pushyamitra founded the Sunga dynasty and the Kanva dynasty was founded by Vasudeva Kanva (कण्व वंश — संस्थापक वासुदेव, पुष्यमित्र नहीं)

 

• Vasudeva was the minister who murdered the last Sunga king Devabhuti.

 

• The Kanva dynasty ruled for only about 45 years.

 

• Its last ruler Susharman is said to have been defeated by the Satavahanas.

 

• Pataliputra remained the Kanva capital.

 

• Always read NOT-type questions carefully, because one false statement is hidden among three true ones.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sunga to Kanva is a change of dynasty by a minister's coup, not by conquest from outside.

 

• Kanva territory was limited mainly to Magadha and nearby areas.

 

• The Satavahanas filled the political space left in central India.

 

• The Kanva dynasty ruled from about 73 BC to 28 BC; after it Magadha ceased to be a major political centre until the rise of the Guptas.

 

NOTE

 

• It was founded by Vasudeva Kanva (Option 1): That the dynasty was founded by Vasudeva Kanva is correct, as he overthrew the last Sunga king. Since the question asks for the incorrect statement, this true statement cannot be the answer.

 

• It ruled for about 45 years (Option 2): That the Kanvas ruled for about 45 years is a correct statement from the Puranic tradition. As it is true, it is not the answer to a NOT-type question.

 

• Its last ruler was Susharman (Option 4): That Susharman was the last Kanva ruler is correct, so this statement is true. A NOT-type question requires the false statement, which is not this one.

question:
Assertion (A): The Sunga dynasty came to an end during the reign of Devabhuti.

Reason (R): Devabhuti was murdered by his minister Vasudeva Kanva, who founded a new dynasty.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both are true and R explains A: Devabhuti was killed by his own minister Vasudeva Kanva, and this murder ended the Sunga line and began the Kanva dynasty (देवभूति की हत्या — शुंग वंश का अंत)

 

• The Sunga rule had lasted roughly a century after Pushyamitra.

 

• The change was a palace coup rather than a foreign conquest.

 

• The Kanvas then ruled for about 45 years from Pataliputra.

 

• The Kanva dynasty in turn gave way to rising Satavahana power.

 

• Remember that the murder of Devabhuti ended a Sunga rule of about a century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sunga capital: Pataliputra / Vidisha.

 

• Sunga founder: Pushyamitra; priest: Patanjali.

 

• Heliodorus's Besnagar pillar belongs to Sunga territory.

 

• Sunga kings are credited with a Vedic revival, yet Buddhist art also flourished at Bharhut and Sanchi during their rule.

 

• Kanva kings ruled around 73 to 28 BC from Pataliputra, so the Sunga fall and Kanva rise took place about the middle of the first century BC.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): This option says R is true but not the explanation. In fact the murder of Devabhuti by Vasudeva Kanva is exactly the event that ended the dynasty, so R directly explains A.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): This option calls A true and R false. Both are true, since Devabhuti did end the line and the murder by his minister Vasudeva Kanva is a fact.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This option claims A is false and R true. A is also true, because the Sunga line truly ended with Devabhuti, so A cannot be false.

question:
Match the following:

(a) Pushyamitra  (i) Last Sunga ruler

(b) Patanjali  (ii) Founder of Kanva dynasty

(c) Vasudeva  (iii) Author of Mahabhasya

(d) Devabhuti  (iv) Founder of Sunga dynasty
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i: Pushyamitra founded the Sunga dynasty, Patanjali wrote the Mahabhasya, Vasudeva founded the Kanva dynasty and Devabhuti was the last Sunga king (पुष्यमित्र, पतंजलि, वासुदेव, देवभूति)

 

• Pushyamitra was originally the commander of the last Maurya, Brihadratha.

 

• Patanjali wrote his commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi.

 

• Vasudeva was the minister of Devabhuti before he seized power.

 

• Devabhuti was the last of the Sunga line.

 

• Remember the order of Magadhan rule after the Mauryas: Sunga first, then Kanva, and the Kanva dynasty was founded by killing the last Sunga king.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sunga period c. 185 BC - 73 BC; Kanva period c. 73 BC - 28 BC.

 

• Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedhas.

 

• Kanva dynasty ended with Susharman.

 

• Sunga rule is dated roughly from 185 BC to 73 BC and Kanva rule from 73 BC to 28 BC.

 

• Heliodorus, the Greek envoy who erected the Garuda pillar at Besnagar, came to the court at Vidisha during the Sunga age.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This pattern makes Pushyamitra the author of the Mahabhasya and Patanjali the Sunga founder, which is reversed. Pushyamitra founded the dynasty while Patanjali was merely his priest and grammarian.

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i (Option 2): This pattern calls Patanjali the founder of the Kanva dynasty and Vasudeva the author of the Mahabhasya. Both are wrong, since Vasudeva was the Kanva founder and Patanjali the grammarian.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-iv, d-ii (Option 3): This pattern calls Pushyamitra the last Sunga ruler and Devabhuti the Kanva founder, reversing the facts. Pushyamitra was the first Sunga king and Devabhuti the last, killed by Vasudeva Kanva.

question: Who was the founder of the Satavahana dynasty of the Deccan?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Simuka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Simuka was the founder of the Satavahana dynasty, which rose in the Deccan after the decline of the Mauryas (सिमुक — सातवाहन वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• Tradition says Simuka overthrew the last Kanva ruler Susharman and extended Satavahana power.

 

• The Satavahanas are also called Andhras in the Puranas, and ruled mainly over the Deccan (present Maharashtra and Andhra).

 

• Their greatest ruler was Gautamiputra Satakarni and the last great ruler was Yajna Sri Satakarni.

 

• They promoted trade with Rome and patronised both Brahmanical and Buddhist faiths.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Satavahana rule is placed from about the 1st century BC to the 3rd century AD.

 

• Satavahana kings used metronymics, naming themselves after their mothers, e.g. Gautamiputra and Vashishthiputra.

 

• Nasik, Karle and Nanaghat are important Satavahana-era sites with inscriptions.

 

• The Satavahana kingdom is often seen as the first major power to fill the political gap in the Deccan after the Mauryan decline.

 

• Satavahana rule over the Deccan is usually dated from the first century BC to the third century AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni (Option 1): Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest Satavahana king, but he ruled generations after the dynasty began. He is famous for reviving the dynasty, not for founding it.

 

• Yajna Sri Satakarni (Option 2): Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great Satavahana ruler, from the later phase of the dynasty. He therefore marks the end of its glory, not the beginning.

 

• Vindhyashakti (Option 4): Vindhyashakti was the founder of the Vakataka dynasty, which rose after the Satavahanas in central India. He belongs to a different dynasty and a different period.

question: Gautamiputra Satakarni, who ruled in the early centuries AD, is regarded as the greatest among the rulers of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satavahana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest ruler of the Satavahana dynasty, remembered for defeating the Sakas and restoring Satavahana power (गौतमीपुत्र शातकर्णी — सातवाहन)

 

• His reign is placed in the early 2nd century AD (about 106 to 130 AD in the notes).

 

• His achievements are recorded in the Nasik inscription issued by his mother Gautami Balashri.

 

• He is described as the destroyer of the Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.

 

• He was succeeded by his son Vashishthiputra Pulamayi.

 

• Gautamiputra's victories over the Sakas restored the prestige of the dynasty that had earlier suffered from Saka pressure in the west.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Satavahana kings were known by metronymics (names from mothers).

 

• Their kingdom stretched across the Deccan from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal.

 

• Satavahanas patronised Prakrit literature such as Hala's Gathasaptashati.

 

• The Nasik inscription of Gautami Balashri is the key epigraphic source for his reign and conquests.

 

• Satavahana trade flourished with the Roman world through western ports.

 

NOTE

 

• Gupta (Option 2): The Guptas ruled in the 4th to 6th centuries AD, far later than Gautamiputra. Their greatest rulers were Samudragupta and Chandragupta II.

 

• Sunga (Option 3): The Sungas ruled in Magadha from about 185 BC and had no link with Gautamiputra. Their rule ended long before his time, and their key figure was Pushyamitra.

 

• Kushana (Option 4): The Kushanas were a Central Asian dynasty of north-west India whose greatest ruler was Kanishka. Gautamiputra ruled in the Deccan and was a Satavahana, not a Kushana.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Satavahanas:

1. Simuka was the founder of the dynasty.

2. Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest ruler of the dynasty.

3. Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great Satavahana ruler.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Simuka founded the dynasty, Gautamiputra Satakarni was its greatest ruler and Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great ruler (सिमुक, गौतमीपुत्र, यज्ञश्री शातकर्णी)

 

• The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan and are also called Andhras.

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni is known for his victory over the Sakas.

 

• Yajna Sri Satakarni issued coins with a ship motif, showing sea trade.

 

• After the Satavahanas, local dynasties took control of different parts of the Deccan.

 

• Remember the three milestones of the dynasty in order: founder Simuka, greatest ruler Gautamiputra and last great ruler Yajna Sri.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• An early Satavahana capital was Pratishthana (Paithan).

 

• They used the Prakrit language in inscriptions.

 

• Their coinage included lead and potin pieces.

 

• The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan for several centuries and are called Andhras in the Puranas.

 

• Their later rulers gave way to Ikshvakus, Abhiras, Vakatakas and Pallavas.

 

• Satavahana kings issued lead coins as well as silver and copper pieces bearing names and symbols.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): This pairing accepts statements 1 and 2 but rejects statement 3. Statement 3 is also correct, because Yajna Sri Satakarni is regarded as the last great Satavahana ruler.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This selection accepts statements 2 and 3 only and rejects statement 1. Statement 1 is also correct since Simuka founded the dynasty, so it cannot be left out.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Here the option accepts statements 1 and 3 but rejects statement 2. Statement 2 is correct, as Gautamiputra Satakarni was the dynasty's greatest king, so leaving it out is wrong.

question: Who succeeded Gautamiputra Satakarni on the Satavahana throne?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vashishthiputra Pulamayi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vashishthiputra Pulamayi was the son and successor of Gautamiputra Satakarni on the Satavahana throne (वशिष्ठीपुत्र पुलमावि — गौतमीपुत्र का पुत्र)

 

• He continued Satavahana rule over the Deccan after his father's reign.

 

• Like his father, he used a metronymic, naming himself after his mother.

 

• Under him, the Satavahanas faced pressure from the Western Kshatrapa Saka rulers.

 

• The last great ruler of the line was Yajna Sri Satakarni.

 

• Gautamiputra's mother Gautami Balashri recorded his victories in the Nasik inscription, a useful source for exam questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rudradaman of the Sakas is said to have defeated a Satavahana king in the Junagadh inscription.

 

• Matrimonial ties between Satavahanas and Kshatrapas are mentioned in sources.

 

• Satavahana inscriptions use Prakrit in the Brahmi script.

 

• Satavahana kings took names from their mothers, such as Gautamiputra and Vashishthiputra, a feature called metronymic.

 

• The dynasty faced the Western Kshatrapa Sakas in a long struggle over Gujarat, Malwa and the Konkan coast.

 

• After Yajna Sri Satakarni, the empire declined and broke into regional kingdoms.

 

NOTE

 

• Yajna Sri Satakarni (Option 1): Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great ruler of the dynasty, reigning generations later. He did not directly succeed Gautamiputra.

 

• Simuka (Option 3): Simuka was the very first Satavahana king and the founder of the dynasty. He lived long before Gautamiputra, so he could not follow him on the throne.

 

• Vasudeva (Option 4): Vasudeva Kanva founded the Kanva dynasty in Magadha and was never a Satavahana. He lived long before the era of Gautamiputra's successor.

question: Who was the last great ruler of the Satavahana dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yajna Sri Satakarni.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great ruler of the Satavahana dynasty; after him the empire broke up (यज्ञश्री शातकर्णी — अंतिम महान सातवाहन शासक)

 

• He revived Satavahana prestige and held territory in both the east and west of the Deccan.

 

• His coins carry a ship motif, which points to Satavahana sea trade.

 

• After him the dynasty declined and local powers took over.

 

• The Ikshvakus, Abhiras, Vakatakas and Pallavas rose in different regions.

 

• After Yajna Sri Satakarni the Satavahana empire rapidly shrank and finally disappeared in the third century AD.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pliny the Elder mentions the Andhras as a powerful people with many walled towns.

 

• The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea records ports and trade of the Deccan.

 

• Roman gold coins (aurei) found in the Deccan reflect Indo-Roman trade.

 

• Satavahana coins with ship motifs show interest in sea trade and overseas contacts.

 

• The Satavahana period saw the growth of port towns on both the western and eastern coasts of the Deccan.

 

• Roman trade brought gold and other valuable goods into the Deccan in this age.

 

NOTE

 

• Simuka (Option 1): Simuka founded the Satavahana dynasty and thus began it. The question asks for the last great ruler, who reigned several centuries later.

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni (Option 2): Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest ruler but not the last great one. He reigned in the early 2nd century AD, before Yajna Sri.

 

• Vashishthiputra Pulamayi (Option 3): Vashishthiputra Pulamayi was the son and successor of Gautamiputra, an important but earlier king. He came before Yajna Sri and is not called the last great ruler.

question: The Satavahana kings were succeeded by the rulers of which dynasty in the Andhra region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ikshvaku dynasty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Krishna-Guntur region (Andhra) the Satavahanas were succeeded by the Ikshvaku dynasty, who continued patronage of Buddhism and Brahmanism (इक्ष्वाकु वंश — कृष्णा-गुंटूर क्षेत्र)

 

• The Ikshvakus ruled from the 3rd century AD and are known from the sites at Nagarjunakonda.

 

• Other successors were the Abhiras in Maharashtra and western Deccan, the Vakatakas in Vidarbha and central India, and the Pallavas in the south-east Deccan.

 

• Satavahana power thus broke into regional kingdoms after Yajna Sri.

 

• This fragmentation prepared the ground for later Deccan powers.

 

• Note that Nagarjunakonda in the Krishna valley is the best known Ikshvaku site and has many Buddhist remains.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nagarjunakonda (Andhra) has Buddhist stupas and viharas of the Ikshvaku period.

 

• The Vakatakas were contemporaries of the Guptas.

 

• The Pallavas later became major rulers of Kanchipuram.

 

• Vakatakas were closely linked with the Guptas, as Chandragupta II gave his daughter to a Vakataka prince.

 

• Many of the successor dynasties emerged from the officers and local chiefs of the Satavahana empire.

 

NOTE

 

• Maurya dynasty (Option 2): The Maurya dynasty preceded the Satavahanas by centuries, ending in 185 BC with Brihadratha. A dynasty that came earlier cannot be a successor.

 

• Nanda dynasty (Option 3): The Nanda dynasty ruled Magadha in the 4th century BC and was destroyed by Chandragupta Maurya. It came long before the Satavahanas and ruled elsewhere.

 

• Shishunaga dynasty (Option 4): The Shishunaga dynasty belonged to the 5th and 4th centuries BC in Magadha, even earlier than the Mauryas. It cannot be a successor of the Satavahanas.

question:
Match the successors of the Satavahanas with the regions they controlled:

(a) Ikshvaku  (i) Maharashtra and western Deccan

(b) Abhira  (ii) Vidarbha and central India

(c) Vakataka  (iii) Krishna-Guntur region

(d) Pallava  (iv) South-eastern Deccan
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv: Ikshvakus ruled the Krishna-Guntur region, Abhiras Maharashtra and the western Deccan, Vakatakas Vidarbha and central India, and Pallavas the south-eastern Deccan (इक्ष्वाकु, आभीर, वाकाटक, पल्लव)

 

• After the Satavahanas, power in the Deccan became regional.

 

• The Vakatakas were contemporaries of the Gupta dynasty.

 

• The Pallavas later made Kanchipuram their capital.

 

• The Ikshvakus are linked with Nagarjunakonda.

 

• Remember the region pairs: Ikshvaku with Andhra, Abhira with Maharashtra, Vakataka with Vidarbha and central India, and Pallava with the south-east.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vakataka founder: Vindhyashakti.

 

• Abhira rulers are linked in inscriptions with the Nasik region.

 

• The Pallavas rose to power in the south-eastern Deccan before the Imperial Pallavas of Kanchipuram.

 

• The Ikshvakus are known from inscriptions at Nagarjunakonda in the Krishna valley.

 

• The Abhiras held the Nasik region and parts of Maharashtra after the Satavahana decline.

 

• The Pallavas later grew into a strong dynasty with Kanchipuram as capital.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 1): This pairing gives Ikshvaku the Maharashtra region and Abhira the Krishna-Guntur region, which swaps them. Ikshvakus ruled Andhra's Krishna-Guntur area, while Abhiras held Maharashtra.

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 2): This pairing keeps Ikshvaku correct but swaps Vakataka and Abhira; Vakatakas held Vidarbha and central India, not Maharashtra and the western Deccan.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii (Option 3): This pairing assigns the south-east Deccan to Ikshvaku and the Krishna-Guntur region to Pallava, reversing both. The Pallavas ruled the south-east, while Ikshvakus ruled Krishna-Guntur.

question: Who was the founder of the Vakataka dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vindhyashakti.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vindhyashakti was the founder of the Vakataka dynasty, which rose in central India and the Deccan after the Satavahanas (विंध्यशक्ति — वाकाटक वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• The Puranas refer to the Vakatakas as the Vindhyakas, a name linked with the founder.

 

• The Vakatakas were contemporaries of the Guptas; the Gupta king Chandragupta II married his daughter into the Vakataka house.

 

• They controlled Vidarbha and central India.

 

• Their rule is famous for the Buddhist paintings at Ajanta in the later phase.

 

• Remember that the Vakataka founder Vindhyashakti is named in the Puranas as the Vindhyaka chief.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harishena was a later Vakataka king under whom Ajanta cave work flourished.

 

• Pravarasena I was the most powerful early Vakataka ruler and performed many Vedic sacrifices.

 

• Chandragupta II's daughter Prabhavatigupta married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II.

 

• The Vakataka kings were Hindu rulers who performed Vedic sacrifices and also supported Buddhist monks and caves.

 

• The Ajanta caves near Aurangabad preserve some of the finest ancient Indian paintings.

 

NOTE

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni (Option 1): Gautamiputra Satakarni was a Satavahana ruler, not a Vakataka. The Vakatakas came after the Satavahanas and had no connection with him.

 

• Harishena (Option 3): Harishena was a later Vakataka ruler of the Vatsagulma branch, under whom Ajanta flourished. He was a descendant and not the founder.

 

• Pravarasena I (Option 4): Pravarasena I was the most powerful early Vakataka king and performed several Vedic sacrifices. He came after Vindhyashakti, who laid the foundation of the dynasty.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Vakatakas:

1. They came after the Satavahanas.

2. They were contemporaries of the Guptas.

3. The founder of the dynasty was Gautamiputra Satakarni.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The true statements here are 1 and 2: the Vakatakas followed the Satavahanas and were contemporaries of the Guptas; statement 3 is wrong as the founder was Vindhyashakti (वाकाटक — सातवाहनों के बाद, गुप्तों के समकालीन)

 

• The Puranas call the Vakatakas the Vindhyakas.

 

• They controlled Vidarbha and central India.

 

• A marriage link joined the Vakatakas and the Gupta king Chandragupta II.

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni belonged to the Satavahana dynasty.

 

• The Vakatakas ruled over Vidarbha and central India with capitals such as Nandivardhana and Vatsagulma.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ajanta caves were patronised in part by Vakataka rulers and their ministers.

 

• The Vakatakas were Brahmanical in faith but tolerant to Buddhism.

 

• Prabhavatigupta ruled as regent for her sons.

 

• The Vakatakas were Brahmanical in religion, but their ministers also built Buddhist caves at Ajanta.

 

• Chandragupta II strengthened his southern frontier by marrying his daughter to a Vakataka prince.

 

• The Vakataka power declined in the later sixth century AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): The chosen option takes statements 2 and 3 as correct, but statement 3 names Gautamiputra as founder, which is wrong, while statement 1 is right.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This alternative takes statements 1 and 3 as correct, but statement 3 is false and statement 2 is true, so it fails.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This response counts all three as correct, but statement 3 is false because Vindhyashakti and not Gautamiputra Satakarni founded the Vakatakas.

question: The Satavahana dynasty ruled mainly over which part of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Deccan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Satavahanas ruled mainly over the Deccan (present Maharashtra and Andhra regions) in the centuries after the Mauryas (सातवाहन — दक्कन क्षेत्र)

 

• They are known in the Puranas as Andhras.

 

• Their power reached from the Arabian Sea coast in the west to the Bay of Bengal coast in the east.

 

• They are remembered for fostering trade and for patronage of Buddhist and Brahmanical faiths.

 

• Their strongest king Gautamiputra Satakarni checked the Sakas.

 

• The Satavahanas are among the best known early historic Deccan rulers, and questions often ask about their region, founder and greatest king.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• After the Satavahanas, the Deccan split among Ikshvakus, Abhiras, Vakatakas and Pallavas.

 

• Satavahana sites include Nasik, Karle and Amaravati.

 

• Their language of inscriptions was Prakrit.

 

• The Deccan plateau lies between the Narmada in the north and the Krishna-Tungabhadra region in the south.

 

• Satavahana territory touched both the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal coasts.

 

• Satavahanas used the Prakrit language and Brahmi script in their inscriptions.

 

NOTE

 

• The Punjab (Option 2): The Punjab lay in the north-west and was held at various times by Indo-Greeks, Sakas and Kushanas. It was not the base of the Satavahanas, who were a Deccan power.

 

• Bengal (Option 3): Bengal in the east was not the centre of Satavahana power. The Satavahanas were based much farther south and west in the Deccan plateau.

 

• The Indus delta (Option 4): The Indus delta lay in the north-west and came under the Sakas and other foreign rulers. It was not part of the Satavahana heartland.

question: In the middle of the third century BC, Bactria and Parthia broke away from which empire, paving the way for the Indo-Greek rulers?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Seleucid (Syrian) empire.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the middle of the third century BC, Bactria and Parthia broke away from the Seleucid (Syrian) empire, and the Greek rulers of Bactria later pushed into north-western India as the Indo-Greeks (सेल्यूकस साम्राज्य से बैक्ट्रिया-पार्थिया का अलगाव)

 

• The Seleucid empire had been founded by Seleucus Nicator, a general of Alexander, who also sent Megasthenes to the court of Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• Once free of Seleucid control, the Bactrian Greeks became strong enough to cross the Hindu Kush and attack Afghanistan and the Punjab.

 

• These Bactrian Greek invaders are called Indo-Greeks or Bactrians in Indian history books, and they were the first of the foreign dynasties after the Mauryas.

 

• They were followed in north-western India by the Sakas, Parthians and Kushanas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Seleucus I Nicator ruled a vast area from Syria to the Indus after Alexander's death.

 

• Chandragupta Maurya defeated Seleucus and received the north-western provinces in exchange for 500 elephants.

 

• The Indo-Greek period brought Greek coinage styles, with the king's portrait and bilingual legends, into India.

 

• Bactria lay in the region of northern Afghanistan and Central Asia, beyond the Hindu Kush mountains.

 

NOTE

 

• Mauryan empire (Option 1): The Mauryan empire was an Indian power that ruled Magadha and most of the subcontinent. Bactria and Parthia were never Mauryan provinces that broke away; they were Greek-held lands to the north-west.

 

• Achaemenid empire (Option 2): The Achaemenid empire of Persia had ended long before, when Alexander conquered it in the fourth century BC. It could not be the empire from which Bactria and Parthia separated in the third century BC.

 

• Roman empire (Option 4): The Roman empire arose far to the west and did not rule Central Asia in the third century BC. It had no role in the revolt of Bactria and Parthia.

question: Which Greek ruler of Bactria invaded and occupied Afghanistan and the Punjab, sending his commanders Apollodotus and Menander to conquer further?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Demetrius.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Demetrius, the Greek ruler of Bactria, invaded and occupied Afghanistan and the Punjab, and from Taxila he sent two commanders, Apollodotus and Menander, to conquer more territory (डेमेट्रियस — बैक्ट्रिया का यूनानी शासक)

 

• His conquests made the Indo-Greeks the first foreign dynasty to rule large parts of north-western India after the Mauryas.

 

• Taxila, in the Gandhara region, served as the base from which his generals advanced further into India.

 

• Among his commanders, Menander later became the most famous Indo-Greek king and ruled from the Punjab.

 

• The Indo-Greek hold on the north-west later weakened under pressure from the Sakas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Menander is also known by his Indian name Milinda.

 

• Indo-Greek coins carried portraits of kings and legends in Greek and Kharosthi.

 

• The Besnagar Garuda pillar was set up by Heliodorus, an envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas.

 

• Demetrius is sometimes linked with the city of Sakala (Sialkot) in the Punjab as an Indo-Greek centre.

 

• The Indo-Greeks ruled in many small kingdoms at the same time, often in conflict with each other.

 

NOTE

 

• Antiochus (Option 2): Antiochus was a Seleucid ruler of the Syrian empire, not the Bactrian king who invaded Afghanistan and the Punjab. The Bactrians had broken away from the empire of the Antiochus family.

 

• Heliodorus (Option 3): Heliodorus was the Greek envoy of King Antialcidas who set up the Garuda pillar at Besnagar. He was a diplomat who became a Vaishnava, not the conqueror of Afghanistan and the Punjab.

 

• Seleucus (Option 4): Seleucus Nicator founded the Seleucid empire and had dealings with Chandragupta Maurya. He lived earlier than the Bactrian rulers and did not conquer the Punjab in this period.

question:
Consider the following statements about Menander:

1. He is also known as Milinda.

2. He converted to Buddhism under the influence of the monk Nagasena.

3. His capital was Purushapura, modern Peshawar.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only statements 1 and 2 hold true: Menander is also called Milinda and became a Buddhist under the influence of Nagasena; statement 3 is wrong because Purushapura was the capital of the Kushana king Kanishka (मिनांडर/मिलिंद — नागसेन के प्रभाव से बौद्ध)

 

• Menander was an Indo-Greek ruler who first served as a commander of Demetrius and later ruled in the north-west.

 

• The Pali work Milinda Panho (Questions of Milinda) records his philosophical dialogue with the Buddhist monk Nagasena.

 

• His rule is remembered for his interest in Buddhism and for his coins, which are among the first gold coins in India.

 

• Purushapura, today's Peshawar, was the capital of Kanishka, and this is the detail that makes statement 3 false.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Menander's coins have been found over a wide area of north-western India.

 

• Nagasena was a learned Buddhist monk whose replies to the king form the substance of the Milinda Panho.

 

• Milinda Panho is a prose text in the Pali language.

 

• Menander's coins show him as a helmeted king and carry the Buddhist wheel symbol on some issues.

 

• He is regarded as the greatest of the Indo-Greek kings of India.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This grouping accepts statement 3 together with statement 2, but statement 3 is false because Peshawar (Purushapura) was Kanishka's capital. It also drops statement 1, which is true.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This choice accepts statements 1 and 3 but drops statement 2. Statement 2 is true, as Menander became a Buddhist under Nagasena, and statement 3 is wrong because Purushapura belongs to Kanishka.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): This answer accepts all three statements, but statement 3 is wrong, since Menander did not make Purushapura his capital; that city is linked to the Kushana ruler Kanishka.

question: The Milinda Panho, recording the questions of the Indo-Greek king Milinda (Menander) to a Buddhist monk, was composed in which language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Milinda Panho (Questions of Milinda) is a Pali text that records the dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the Buddhist monk Nagasena (मिलिंद पन्हो — पालि भाषा में)

 

• The book discusses Buddhist ideas such as the soul, rebirth and the nature of existence in a question-and-answer form.

 

• Pali was the main language of early Buddhist canonical literature, which is why this work is also written in it.

 

• Menander's interest in Buddhism under the influence of Nagasena is shown in this text, and he is remembered as a patron of the faith.

 

• The text is a valuable source for understanding Indo-Greek contact with Indian religion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pali is the language of the Theravada Buddhist canon, the Tipitaka.

 

• Sanskrit was used for Mahayana works such as the Buddhacharita of Ashvaghosha.

 

• Indo-Greek coins used Greek and Kharosthi legends, not Pali.

 

• The Milinda Panho became a respected non-canonical Pali book of the Theravada Buddhist tradition.

 

• The Pali canon, the Tipitaka, comprises the Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitakas.

 

NOTE

 

• Sanskrit (Option 2): Sanskrit was the language of works such as Ashvaghosha's Buddhacharita and Patanjali's Mahabhasya. The Milinda Panho, however, belongs to the Pali Buddhist tradition, not to the Sanskrit one.

 

• Greek (Option 3): Greek was the native language of Menander and appears on his coins, but the book of his dialogue with Nagasena is an Indian Buddhist text. It was not written in Greek.

 

• Tamil (Option 4): Tamil was the language of the Sangam literature in the far south of India. It has no role in the Milinda Panho, which is a Buddhist text from the north-west composed in Pali.

question: Which ruling group is credited with being the first to issue gold coins in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indo-Greeks.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indo-Greeks, notably Menander, are credited with issuing the first gold coins in India, bearing the king's portrait and legends in Greek and Kharosthi (इंडो-ग्रीक — भारत में सर्वप्रथम स्वर्ण सिक्के)

 

• Before them the Indian coins were mostly punch-marked pieces of silver and copper without royal portraits.

 

• The Kushanas later issued the purest gold coins under Kanishka, and the Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins.

 

• The sequence to remember is: first gold coins - Indo-Greeks; purest gold coins - Kushanas; maximum gold coins - Guptas.

 

• Greek influence also brought the use of the king's head and the name of the ruler on coins.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indo-Greek coinage also carried portraits of kings with Greek and Kharosthi inscriptions.

 

• The Kushana gold coins show Greek, Iranian and Indian deities.

 

• Gupta gold coins are called Dinaras.

 

• Earlier Indian coins were punch-marked pieces called karshapanas, mostly made of silver and copper.

 

• Kushana coins followed the Indo-Greek models but used Roman gold standards.

 

NOTE

 

• Mauryas (Option 1): The Mauryas used punch-marked silver and copper coins called karshapanas and did not issue gold coins in the manner of the Indo-Greeks. Their coinage had no royal portraits.

 

• Sungas (Option 3): The Sungas, who ruled in Magadha after the Mauryas, continued earlier traditions of local coinage. They are not credited with introducing gold coins to India.

 

• Satavahanas (Option 4): The Satavahanas issued many lead and potin coins and some silver ones, but they are not known as the first to issue gold coins in India. That credit goes to the Indo-Greeks.
